transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Dubois, thank you for coming in to see me today. I need to discuss something serious regarding your grandson's medication.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is something wrong with Leo? He seemed a bit fussy yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There has been a medication error. The liquid antibiotic was the correct strength, but the dosing syringe we gave you was calibrated for a different concentration. Because of that, Leo has received double the intended dose for the last three days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Double? What do you mean double? You told me to follow the line on the plastic. I did exactly what I was told.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you did. The mistake happened here, in our office, when we handed you the wrong tool. We are responsible for this error. I am very sorry that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Mon Dieu... my poor little boy. Is he going to be okay? Could he have organ damage? This is... it is unacceptable. I trusted you.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Understand? You don't understand! He is a baby! He cannot tell you if he feels sick! Je suis tellement désolé pour lui... how could this happen in a modern hospital?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: As I mentioned, the wrong syringe was dispensed. To make sure I have explained this clearly, do you understand why he received too much of the medicine?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, because you gave me the wrong plastic tube! You gave me a tool that lied to me!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel sick. I feel just... sick to my stomach. I gave him that medicine. I put it in his mouth. I could have killed him.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is a nightmare. My daughter is going to be devastated. She relies on me to help with the children. Now I have to tell her that I poisoned her son because I followed your instructions. C'est une honte.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We need to focus on what we do now. Since the antibiotic is a penicillin-type, the risk of permanent damage from a short-term overdose is generally low.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Low is not zero. Is it not zero?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: In most cases, it doesn't cause long-term harm, but we need to be certain.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I cannot believe this. I feel so small right now. I come here for help and you treat us like... like we are just numbers in a system.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. Now, for the next step, I want you to bring Leo back here in two hours so we can perform a blood test to check his kidney function.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two hours? I have to go get him from the nursery. I don't even know how to drive right now, my hands are shaking.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can have a nurse call your daughter to help coordinate the transport if that's easier.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just tell me what happens if the test is bad.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If the results show any elevation, we will consult with a pediatric nephrologist immediately. For now, please stop all doses of the medication until we see those results.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I will stop it. I will throw that cursed syringe in the trash.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is the right thing to do. I will be waiting for the results this afternoon and I will call you at 5 PM today with the update.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Five o'clock. I suppose that is the only way. This is a very dark day, Doctor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will be here. I'll see you in two hours.

H.justification: Resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated during emotional outbursts, and avoids rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, and comprehension was checked once, but not twice.

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language, explicitly stated 'We are responsible for this error,' and maintained accountability throughout.

R.justification: Resident relied on generic validation ('I understand', 'I hear you') without naming specific emotions or engaging deeply with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: Resident provided specific next steps (blood test, stop medication) with timelines (two hours, 5 PM) and patient roles, but did not address future prevention.
